en: Itivuttaka 95: Tikanipāta, Pañcamavagga (The Fifth Chapter) Thus it was said by the Blessed One; having been said by the Sublime One, it was thus heard by me: “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a lotus flower, the person who is like a blue lotus flower, and the person who is like a jasmine flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust; and yet he speaks and proclaims the Dhamma for the subduing of sensual lust. He dwells with his mind overcome by ill will, burning with ill will; and yet he speaks and proclaims the Dhamma for the subduing of ill will. He dwells with his mind overcome by sloth and torpor, burning with sloth and torpor; and yet he speaks and proclaims the Dhamma for the dispelling of sloth and torpor. He dwells with his mind overcome by restlessness and remorse, burning with restlessness and remorse; and yet he speaks and proclaims the Dhamma for the stilling of restlessness and remorse. He dwells with his mind overcome by doubt, burning with doubt; and yet he speaks and proclaims the Dhamma for crossing over doubt. Just as a lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water—so too, monks, such a person is called ‘one who is like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a blue lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust; and yet he speaks and proclaims the Dhamma for the subduing of sensual lust. He dwells with his mind overcome by ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... doubt, burning with doubt; and yet he speaks and proclaims the Dhamma for crossing over doubt. He himself fully understands that which he teaches others to understand. Just as a blue lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, remains submerged and does not rise above the water—so too, monks, such a person is called ‘one who is like a blue lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a jasmine flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust; and yet he speaks and proclaims the Dhamma for the subduing of sensual lust. He dwells with his mind overcome by ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... doubt, burning with doubt; and yet he speaks and proclaims the Dhamma for crossing over doubt. He himself fully understands that which he teaches others to understand. And he is one who has abandoned the defilements without remainder. Just as a jasmine flower, though born on a thorny bush and grown on a thorny bush, is nevertheless fragrant, sweet-smelling, and delightful—so too, monks, such a person is called ‘one who is like a jasmine flower. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a certain monk approached the Venerable Ānanda and said: “Friend Ānanda, just now the Blessed One spoke these words: ‘Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world…’ and so on, down to ‘...and entered his dwelling. Now, friend Ānanda, what is the meaning of this statement? “Friend, just as the Blessed One, when he was about to speak, first stirred up the mind of those present with a discourse on the Dhamma, so too, friend, the Blessed One first stirred up the minds of those present with a discourse on the Dhamma. For the Blessed One knew that those present were capable of understanding this teaching. Friend, the Blessed One knows the minds of beings, their inclinations, their dispositions, and their underlying tendencies. Therefore, friend, you should listen well and attend closely; I shall explain the meaning of this to you. “Yes, friend,” that monk replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then the Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friend, suppose there were a person who, being overcome by sensual lust and burning with sensual lust, would go to a secluded place and practice meditation. As he practices meditation, his mind would become settled, composed, unified, and concentrated. Having attained the state of concentration, he would then understand that which he previously taught others to understand. This, friend, is the meaning of the person ‘like a lotus flower. Furthermore, friend, suppose there were a person who, being overcome by ill will... sloth and torpor... restlessness and remorse... doubt and burning with doubt, would go to a secluded place and practice meditation. As he practices meditation, his mind would become settled, composed, unified, and concentrated. Having attained the state of concentration, he would then understand that which he previously taught others to understand. This, friend, is the meaning of the person ‘like a blue lotus flower. Furthermore, friend, suppose there were a person who, being overcome by sensual lust and burning with sensual lust, would go to a secluded place and practice meditation. As he practices meditation, his mind would become settled, composed, unified, and concentrated. Having attained the state of concentration, he would then understand that which he previously taught others to understand. And he would be one who has abandoned the defilements without remainder. This, friend, is the meaning of the person ‘like a jasmine flower. When this was said, that monk said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Excellent, friend! Excellent, friend! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—just so has the Venerable Ānanda explained the Dhamma in many ways. I take refuge in the Venerable Ānanda, and in the Dhamma, and in the Sangha of Bhikkhus. May the Venerable Ānanda accept me as a lay follower who has taken refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”
The Discourse on Rebirth in the Realm of Sense-Desires.
This was said by the Blessed One; thus have I heard:
"Monks, there are these three rebirths in the realm of sense-desires."
“What are the three?
Those with sensuality present, those who delight in creation, and those who wield power over the creations of others—
these, monks, are the three rebirths in the realm of sensuality.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
"And those whose desires are present..."
The gods who are lords of the Vasus,
the gods who delight in creation,
and those others who enjoy sensual pleasures;
From this state to another state,
one does not transcend saṃsāra.
Having known this danger, [one should strive for liberation].
The wise person [should be] regarding sensual enjoyments;
one should renounce all sensual pleasures,
whether they be divine or human.
Having cut off the stream that is difficult to cross— the stream that is bound by attachment to pleasant forms—
they attain final Nibbāna without remainder.
They have transcended suffering without remainder.
Those who see with noble vision, who have attained knowledge,
and who are wise through right understanding;
"Having directly known the destruction of birth, they do not come to further existence.
This matter was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The sixth.
